summary: The feature profiles the Elm Street Urban Garden Project, a community-led effort that turned a former dump site into a productive garden after launching on September 12, 2023. It covers the volunteers, business partnerships, educational programs, first harvest, health benefits and youth involvement, and ends with plans to replicate the model in other districts by the close of 2024.
one_line: The Elm Street Urban Garden Project turned a vacant dump lot into a thriving community garden with education, business partnerships, youth involvement and expansion plans.
key_facts: The Elm Street Urban Garden Project launched on September 12, 2023, in a vacant lot on Elm Street that had long served as a makeshift dump site.
Environmental advocate and local resident Sandra Jeffries conceived the project, beginning with a modest proposal to the city council.
Volunteers include engineer-turned-composter Nick Patel and retired school teacher Mary Gonzalez.
GreenWay Supplies, a local business, donated tools, seeds and expertise that proved instrumental in the early stages.
Nick Patel oversees the garden's composting program and vertical gardening systems, which maximize yield in limited space.

Mary Gonzalez leads educational programming, including workshops on composting and water conservation, and a grant from the Tomorrow's Green Fund let her add afterschool sessions and weekend workshops.
The Sunnyside Café supplies organic waste for compost and in return uses fresh garden produce in its dishes, an example of a circular economy.
HighRise Tech allocates employee volunteer time for garden maintenance; community outreach coordinator Jared Kim calls it "team building with a purpose."
The first harvest festival took place in October 2023, and surplus produce was donated to the local food bank.
A study by the city's Department of Public Health found participants reported significant improvements in physical and mental health.
Sixteen-year-old environmental club president Zoe Tran and other youth introduced rainwater harvesting systems and a seed exchange program.
The GreenWay initiative is leading a plan to replicate the model, with proposals for three new gardens to be presented to the city council by the close of 2024.
